subChunks.title: The Utility Mindset
subChunks.hookHtml: Every senior front-end developer has a moment when they stop writing custom CSS for each new element and realise that utility-first CSS is faster, more consistent, and far easier to maintain. That moment starts here.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Why utility-first wins

Traditional CSS workflows ask you to do two jobs at once: design the element and invent a name for it. The name ends up in two files — the HTML and the stylesheet — and they must stay in sync forever. Rename one, the other breaks silently.

/* styles.css — the old way */
.profile-card-header-meta-subtitle {
  font-size: 0.875rem;
  color: #6b7280;
  margin-top: 4px;
}

Utility-first removes the naming step entirely. You compose small, single-purpose classes directly on the element:

<p class="text-sm text-gray-500 mt-1">Senior Engineer</p>

Same result. No extra file. No name to maintain.

How does this compare to other approaches?

  • Plain CSS / CSS Modules — maximum flexibility, but you write every value yourself, there is no shared constraint, and design inconsistencies creep in over time.
  • CSS-in-JS (styled-components, Emotion) — co-location is nice, but runtime cost, bundle bloat, and SSR complexity add up fast in production.
  • Semantic CSS (BEM) — disciplined naming helps, but you still maintain two files and the abstraction breaks when the design changes.
  • Tailwind — every token (colour, spacing, type size) is shared across the whole project. Changing the design system means changing one config file, not hundreds of classes.

The property-value naming pattern

Every Tailwind class follows the same pattern: property-value. Once you know the pattern, you can guess new classes before you look them up.

bg-blue-500      /* background-color: rgb(59 130 246)   */
text-white       /* color: rgb(255 255 255)              */
p-4              /* padding: 1rem (16px)                 */
px-6             /* padding-left + right: 1.5rem (24px)  */
rounded-lg       /* border-radius: 0.5rem               */
font-semibold    /* font-weight: 600                    */
shadow-md        /* box-shadow: medium preset           */

Using Tailwind in React

React uses className, not class. This is the only HTML difference you need to remember.

// HTML
<div class="bg-white p-6 rounded-xl shadow-md">

// JSX (React)
<div className="bg-white p-6 rounded-xl shadow-md">

Lyra: "The moment you stop inventing names, you stop maintaining two files. Rename the element? There is nothing to rename — the utilities are the element. Delete the element? The styles vanish with it. No orphaned CSS, no dead code."

storyBeats.text: You step into the Academy's Scriptorium — a vast hall lined with glowing runes. Lyra the Scribe glances up from a stack of scrolls.

storyBeats.speaker: Lyra the Scribe
storyBeats.text: Ah — a new apprentice. Let me guess: you have been writing bespoke names for every scroll you produce? .card-header-title-special, .button-blue-thing-v2? And now you have two scrolls per element — one for the name, one for the spell — and they must stay in sync forever?

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Style this stat card component. Apply the following utilities:

  • .stat-card: bg-white, p-6, rounded-xl, shadow-md, border, border-gray-100
  • .stat-label: text-sm, text-gray-500, font-medium
  • .stat-value: text-3xl, font-bold, text-gray-900, mt-1
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Style this stat card from scratch — no hints. Apply what you know about Tailwind utilities to produce a clean, professional card:

  • The .stat-card needs a white background, comfortable padding, large rounded corners, a subtle shadow, and a thin border.
  • The .stat-label should be small text in a muted colour, medium-weight.
  • The .stat-value should be a very large, bold number in near-black, with a small top margin.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain utility-first CSS to a developer who has only ever used BEM and CSS Modules. Cover: why you do not need to invent class names, how the design system stays consistent, and one scenario where you would still write custom CSS despite using Tailwind.

questions.prompt: Which Tailwind class sets a medium box shadow?
questions.explanation: Shadow utilities follow shadow-{size}: shadow-sm, shadow (default), shadow-md, shadow-lg, shadow-xl, shadow-2xl, shadow-inner, shadow-none.

questions.prompt: A developer writes `className={\`bg-${color}-500\`}` where `color` is a string from an API response. What problem will they encounter?
options: The class will never apply because Tailwind cannot detect dynamically interpolated class names at build time
It works fine — Tailwind handles template literals automatically
It works in development but is slightly slower in production
The class applies but the colour shade will default to 500
questions.answer: The class will never apply because Tailwind cannot detect dynamically interpolated class names at build time
questions.explanation: Tailwind scans source files for complete class name strings. 'bg-blue-500' is found; 'bg-${color}-500' is not. The fix is a lookup map: const colourMap = { blue: 'bg-blue-500', red: 'bg-red-500' }, then use colourMap[color]. This is one of the most common Tailwind gotchas in real projects.

questions.prompt: Your team is debating CSS strategies. The design uses a consistent 8-point spacing scale and a fixed palette of 12 brand colours. Which argument most accurately represents an advantage of Tailwind in this specific context?
options: Tailwind enforces the spacing scale and colour palette automatically through its token system, making design drift structurally impossible without config changes
Tailwind is faster to type than CSS Modules
CSS Modules cannot implement the same design system
Tailwind generates smaller CSS files in all cases
questions.answer: Tailwind enforces the spacing scale and colour palette automatically through its token system, making design drift structurally impossible without config changes
questions.explanation: When a design uses a fixed palette and spacing scale, Tailwind's config is a direct representation of that system. Every developer can only use values that exist in the config — there is nowhere to sneak in an arbitrary color: #e74c3c or margin: 13px. CSS Modules give each developer a blank canvas, which means design drift requires discipline rather than tooling.
